newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Chiroscience gains on cancer drug news.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Chiroscience gains on cancer drug news.

text.p: Shares in biotechnology firm Chiroscience Group Plc climbed seven percent on Monday after the group said it would start human trials with a novel class of cancer drugs which showed "excellent" results in animal tests.
Chiroscience said trials with monkeys showed great effectiveness and selectivity, and none of the side effects seen in tests of similar products of rival companies.
The two new anti-cancer compounds, which are in the same class as British Biotech's potential blockbuster marimastat, are to start clinical trials in the fourth quarter of this year.
The drugs are so-called matrix metalloproteinase inhibitors, a new generation of cancer therapies which do not kill a tumour but instead block its growth.
But unlike marimastat, which is already in the second phase of its human trials, the Chiroscience compounds D1927 and D2163 appear not to cause joint pains.
"We believe that if you have drugs with the same efficacy as marimastat, but not the same side effects, that is clearly an advantage to patients," chief executive John Padfield told Reuters.

The joint pains, which affected about 30 percent of patients taking marimastat after three to five months, is probably caused by Interleukin-1, but Padfield said the chemical is not released by the two Chiroscience drugs.
Chiroscience shares rose to a session high of 442 pence in late morning trade, up 39.5 pence on the day, while British Biotech eased two pence to 257-1/2.
Padfield cautioned, however, against too much optimism over the prospects of the Chrioscience compounds.

"It is early days yet," Padfield said. "The most important stage is to get into clinical trials and check that it is well tolerated and particularly that it does not have the joint pain side effects."
Chiroscience also announced it was considering human trials with new anti-asthma drugs.
These compounds could be developed to become the first drugs to fight both the early and late phases of an asthma attack, Padfield said.
Chiroscience is already in the more advanced stages of developing another PDE IV drug, D4418, which is entering clinical trials by the end of May.

"We shall be showing data today which show that follow-up compounds wipe out both (asthma) phases completely," Padfield said, adding a couple of more months were needed to make decision on whether to start clinical trials.

Chiroscience has one product, the local anaesthetic Levobupivacaine, that is close to coming to the market. Padfield said Chiroscience plans to file for registration in Europe by the end of 1997 and in the United States by April 1998.
He said the anaesthetic, a cleaned-up version of an existing product, was well received in the anaesthetic industry because it proved to be less toxic to the heart than others.
